fields.title: Refusing Part to Save the Rest
fields.keyTakeaway: During overload, dropping part of the requests saves the rest, and the decision on what to drop first is a product decision.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Load is twice the capacity. Serve everyone slowly or half normally?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A system without a shedding mechanism under overload degrades to complete inoperability: queues grow, response time exceeds timeouts, and eventually no one is served. "Everyone slowly" in practice means "no one".
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: [[backpressure|Backpressure]] is a signal to the source to slow down. In queues, it is refusing to accept new work until old work is sorted out. In synchronous calls, it is rejecting with `429`.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: [[load-shedding|Load shedding]] is the conscious rejection of a subset of requests for the sake of the rest's operability. Sounds bad, but the alternative is worse.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: Mechanics are simple: if the system processes 400 requests per second and 800 arrive, without shedding the queue grows infinitely, response time goes beyond timeout, and all 800 get an error after a long wait. With shedding, 400 are served normally, 400 get a fast clear rejection.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: The product part is **what to shed.** This is [[traffic-prioritization|prioritization]], and the product manager does it:
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: *By scenario.* Checkout is more important than viewing history. *By user.* Active clients are more important than bots and scrapers. *By request type.* Writes are more important than reads because reads can be retried.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: Practical hierarchy for a consumer product: completing a started action → starting a new action → viewing → background and analytics.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Separately — **what rejection looks like.** Not "error", but "many orders right now, please try in a minute" with auto-retry. An honest overload message is perceived noticeably better than an incomprehensible glitch.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Priorities that activate when load exceeds 85%:
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/0: Completing a started order — never shed.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/1: Adding to cart, authorization — not shed.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/items/2: Catalog and search — shed at 95%, cached results shown.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Logic: a person who started checkout must finish it. Refusal mid-payment is more expensive than order history unavailability.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Applied three times in six months. In the worst case, the partner dashboard was unavailable for 25 minutes, checkout worked without glitches. Partners didn't complain — they were written to in advance.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Prioritization requires the system to distinguish request types before processing them. If everything goes in a single stream, there is nothing to choose from, and this is an architectural requirement laid down in advance.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: During overload, dropping part of the requests saves the rest, and the decision on what to drop first is a product decision.
